- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are rising steadily, check for over-optimism — true outcomes often overshoot initial peaks then correct, especially after high-event days.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish, model forecasts tend to underestimate true price spikes — adjust upward by 2–5% for high-event periods.
- After a sharp spike in true outcome (e.g., >10% above prior 30d mean), model forecasts often lag by 1–3 days — apply a 1-day lag correction for subsequent forecasts.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model forecasts are prone to mean reversion bias — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% if recent true values show downward drift.
- In high-event periods (≥20 events/30d), model forecasts often fail to capture supply shock magnitude — increase forecast baseline by 3–8% to account for policy-driven volatility.
- If sentiment history shows repeated bearish spikes (e.g., 1.00 or -0.33) followed by model forecasts rising, expect a “reversal lag” — delay forecast peak by 2–5 days and reduce amplitude by 10–15%.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcomes show persistent mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 80), model forecasts should be capped at 80–85 to avoid over-leveraging bullish sentiment.
